While the premise of "babies switched at birth" is a familiar trope in fiction, the story subverts it in a deeply original way. Instead of treating the mix-up as a source of melodrama, panic, or a mystery to be solved, the protagonist quietly accepts the switched baby out of a desperate psychological exhaustion and a desire for "certainty" after a precarious, anxiety-ridden pregnancy. Furthermore, the prose itself avoids cliché expressions, relying instead on fresh, unexpected metaphors and observations (such as comparing a baby's thin cry to "a kettle deciding whether to boil," anesthesia to "a long, featureless country with no roads," and living inside the phrase *we'll see* "the way other people learn to live inside their apartments").
